Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Vignette:
Kofi had always been a man who thrived in high-pressure situations. As a bomb disposal technician, he had spent years honing his skills to stay calm and focused in the face of danger. But it was not an explosion that shattered his sense of control, but a hurricane that ravaged his hometown five years ago. Kofi's family had been lucky to escape with their lives, but the experience left him shaken. He remembered the sound of the wind howling like a chorus of banshees, the walls creaking and groaning as if they would collapse at any moment, and the feeling of utter powerlessness as he huddled with his wife and children in the basement, praying for it to pass. The storm's unpredictability had been terrifying - one minute the winds were calm, the next they were raging like a beast unleashed. In the aftermath of the hurricane, Kofi began to notice that loud noises made him jump. At first, it was just the sound of thunder or a car backfiring, but soon he found himself flinching at any sudden noise - a slammed door, a shout from his child, even the beeping of the microwave. His wife would try to reassure him, but Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling that disaster was lurking around every corner. To manage his growing anxiety, Kofi turned to food. He started eating more and more, using the comfort of familiar tastes and textures to calm his racing mind. His weight began to balloon, and his wife expressed concern, but Kofi just shrugged it off. It was easier to eat than to confront the memories that lurked in the shadows of his mind. As time passed, Kofi became increasingly adept at avoiding anything that might trigger those memories. He stopped going to crowded places, avoided loud events, and even quit his beloved hobby of woodworking because the sound of the power tools was too much for him to bear. His work as a bomb disposal technician began to suffer - he found himself hesitating in situations where he once would have acted with confidence. But despite his best efforts, Kofi's body seemed to react before his mind could catch up. He would find himself sweating and trembling at the slightest provocation, his heart racing like a jackrabbit on steroids. Sometimes, he would even experience flashbacks - sudden, jarring moments where he was transported back to that basement, reliving the terror of the hurricane. When Kofi tried to recall the event, he found himself pushing the memories away before they could fully form. It was as if his mind was trying to protect him from the pain and fear by fragmenting the recollection into disjointed images and sounds. But when he did manage to piece together fragments of that day, a wave of intense rage would wash over him, leaving him feeling shaken and guilty. Lately, Kofi's wife had been noticing changes in his behavior - the way he flinched at every loud noise, the way he avoided social gatherings, the way he seemed to be constantly on edge. She encouraged him to seek help, but Kofi was hesitant - what if therapy couldn't fix him? What if he was forever trapped in this cycle of fear and avoidance? It wasn't until his boss expressed concern about his performance at work that Kofi realized he needed to confront his demons head-on. He made the difficult decision to seek help, hoping against hope that a therapist could guide him through the treacherous landscape of his own mind and back into the life he once knew. As he sat in the waiting room, clutching his worn copy of the PTSD support group pamphlet, Kofi felt a glimmer of determination - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to face the storm within himself.
